captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 13: Earth Processes.

Volcanoes are found all over the world, from Iceland to Indonesia. They are openings where heat escapes from deep inside the Earth. That heat, called geothermal energy, can even generate electricity. Let's explore what's happening beneath our feet, and in the air above us.
The Earth is made of layers. On the outside is the crust, a thin layer of solid rock, up to about 60 kilometres thick.
Below is the mantle. The upper mantle is semi-molten rock called magma. The lower mantle is extremely hot, but the huge pressure keeps it solid.
At the centre is the core, made mainly of iron and nickel. The outer core is liquid metal. The inner core is the hottest layer, but the enormous pressure keeps it solid.

Diagrams often show the crust as one solid piece, but it's actually broken into huge slabs of rock called tectonic plates. They fit together like the pieces of a jigsaw puzzle and rest on the mantle. This is the model of plate tectonics.
Plates are made of two kinds of crust. Oceanic crust is heavy and dense, and forms the ocean floor. Continental crust is less dense, and forms the continents.

The plates are about 100 kilometres thick, and they move very slowly, between 1 and 10 centimetres a year. Scientists believe they move because the hot core heats magma in the mantle, making it rise, spread and sink, dragging the plates along.

sections.title: Movement of tectonic plates

stops.note: Paused after: “At a convergent boundary, plates collide, pushing the land up into fold mountains.”
Paused after: “The point underground where the earthquake starts is the focus. The point on the surface d”

q.prompt: The point on the surface above an earthquake's focus is the…

stops.note: Paused after: “Magma also heats underground water, making hot water and steam. Geothermal power plants us”

q.prompt: Magma that reaches the surface is…

captions: The place where two or more plates meet is a plate boundary. Over millions of years, moving plates can create oceans and mountains and even move continents. At a transform boundary, two plates slide past each other in opposite directions. This can cause earthquakes.
At a divergent boundary, plates move away from each other. Magma rises into the gap, forming volcanoes and valleys.
At a convergent boundary, plates collide, pushing the land up into fold mountains.
The plates are always moving, so the ground is always moving too. Usually we can't feel it. But sometimes the ground shakes violently. That's an earthquake.

Earthquakes often happen at transform boundaries. Friction can make the plates stick, so stress builds up. Eventually the stress is too great, and the plates move suddenly, releasing a huge amount of energy as seismic waves, or shock waves, which make the ground shake.
The point underground where the earthquake starts is the focus. The point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre. Indonesia has many earthquakes, because three plates meet there.

A volcano is a vent in the crust where magma and gases escape. Volcanoes form at weak points, often at divergent and convergent boundaries. Magma is less dense than the solid rock around it, so it rises and is trapped in a magma chamber, where pressure builds up.

When the pressure gets too high, magma pushes up through the vent, and the volcano erupts. Magma that reaches the surface is called lava. Over time, layers of lava and ash build up into a cone. There are about 600 active volcanoes today. Mount Vesuvius destroyed the Roman city of Pompeii almost 2000 years ago.
Magma also heats underground water, making hot water and steam. Geothermal power plants use this thermal energy to generate electricity.
Fold mountains form at convergent boundaries, where two continental plates move towards each other.
The movement forces the rock layers to fold upwards, forming hills, mountains, or even whole mountain ranges.

The Himalayas formed about 50 million years ago when the Indian Plate pushed into the Eurasian Plate. The plates are still colliding, so Mount Everest may still be growing by up to half a centimetre a year! You can model this by gently pushing two sheets of paper together.

stops.note: Paused after: “Scientists have been measuring carbon dioxide in the atmosphere for decades, and the amoun”

q.prompt: Which is a natural source of gases in air?

captions: The Earth is surrounded by a layer of air called the atmosphere. Air is a mixture of gases, and the biggest part, 78 percent, about four-fifths, is nitrogen!
Oxygen, the gas we need to breathe, makes up only about 21 percent. Together, nitrogen and oxygen make up 99 percent of clean, dry air.

The last 1 percent is carbon dioxide and other gases. Even small changes in carbon dioxide have big effects on the Earth. Real air also contains water vapour. The amount, called humidity, is higher on warm days, because warm air holds more water vapour.

The composition of air can change. Natural emissions add gases: a volcanic eruption releases ash, carbon dioxide, water vapour and sulfur dioxide, and every living thing gives off carbon dioxide when it respires.

Pollution changes the air too. Burning fossil fuels in power plants, factories and vehicles releases pollutants such as sulfur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen and tiny particles called particulate matter, which can cause breathing problems. It also increases the carbon dioxide in the air.
Scientists have been measuring carbon dioxide in the atmosphere for decades, and the amount keeps rising. Carbon dioxide traps heat, so more of it causes global warming and climate change.
NASA has attached an instrument called OCO-3 to the International Space Station. It can measure carbon dioxide in the atmosphere 72 thousand times a day!

The data show that tropical forests absorb carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. But when forests are cut down and burnt, more carbon dioxide is released, and fewer trees are left to absorb it. Information like this helps us find solutions to climate change.

sections.title: The water cycle

stops.note: Paused after: “Water then flows across the land as run-off, and collects in rivers, lakes and oceans. Som”

q.prompt: Water vapour cooling into droplets is…

captions: The water cycle describes how water moves continuously around the Earth. First, evaporation: the Sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers, and it turns into water vapour, which rises into the air.
Next, condensation: as water vapour rises, it cools and changes into tiny droplets of water, which collect to form clouds.
As droplets grow larger and heavier, they fall as precipitation, such as rain or snow.
Water then flows across the land as run-off, and collects in rivers, lakes and oceans. Some soaks into the ground to become groundwater, which can also flow back to the sea.
And so the cycle goes on and on: the rain falling on you today could have been in the ocean yesterday! You can model it with warm water in a glass, covered with cling film and topped with ice cubes.
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Which layer of the Earth is the hottest? Pause the video now.
Answer: The inner core.
Question 2: What type of plate boundary forms fold mountains? Pause the video now.
Answer: A convergent boundary – plates collide.
Question 3: Which gas makes up most of the air? Pause the video now.
Answer: Nitrogen – about 78%.
Question 4: Name the process in which water vapour turns into droplets to form clouds. Pause the video now.
Answer: Condensation.
